title: Pranzini (1887)
hookLine: the comments under a trial all say 'hope he rots'; Thérèse prays for a condemned murderer she never met
tomorrow: can a teenager just walk up and ask the pope for something?

lines: SHE DECIDES HE WON'T BE LOST.
cards: A trial is all over the news, and the comments under it say the same thing over and over: hope he rots.
In France, a man named Pranzini is condemned to die for terrible murders, and everything Thérèse hears says he's unrepentant. She has never met him.
She decides he will not be lost, and starts to pray for him, quietly, telling almost no one.

teach.h: I THIRST: A THIRST FOR SOULS.
teach.b: Why him? Not long before, a picture of Jesus on the cross had struck her: blood falling from his hand, and no one hurrying to catch it. Jesus's cry, in the Douay-Rheims, "I thirst," lit in her a thirst for souls.
So she prays for Pranzini, offers small sacrifices, and asks her sister Céline to have a Mass said for him. She asks God for a sign, just for her comfort.
Then a newspaper: at the scaffold, without having made his confession, Pranzini suddenly turned, took the crucifix the priest held out, and kissed its wounds. She calls him her first child.
Praying for him doesn't erase what he did, or the people he harmed. It refuses to decide that anyone is beyond reach. A neighbor tradition carries that same hope.
In a Buddhist sutta, Angulimala, a bandit feared for his killings, meets the Buddha, turns, and becomes a monk.
The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, says: "He whose evil deeds are covered by good deeds, brightens up this world, like the moon when freed from clouds." Shared: nobody is written off.

teach.h: ONE HOPE, TWO WAYS IT COMES.
teach.b: The honest difference: Thérèse's hope rests on God's mercy, asked for by someone else in prayer.
Angulimala turns through his own practice on the Buddha's path, and when people throw stones at him, he is told he's bearing the fruit of his own deeds.

how: Catholics pray for prisoners and for the dying, and visiting the imprisoned is one of the corporal works of mercy; some parishes run prison ministries.

o: the priest who heard her first confession
the condemned man she prayed for, who turned
the town in France where she grew up

p: he kissed it at the scaffold
a bandit who turned, in a Buddhist sutta

s: Pranzini made his confession before he died
he hadn't confessed. at the scaffold he took the crucifix and kissed its wounds.
Thérèse asked God for a sign, just for her own comfort
and the newspaper told her what happened at the scaffold.
the Dhammapada compares a person whose good covers past evil to the moon freed from clouds
it brightens up this world, in Max Müller's translation.

games.q: in world history, your class reads about Angulimala, and someone says, so it's the same story as Thérèse and Pranzini. what's the honest answer?
o: both refuse to write a person off; they differ on how the turn comes.
exactly the same story, just told in two religions.
nothing alike: one is about a monk, one about a criminal.
games.why: both hold that a life that did terrible harm can still turn. Thérèse trusts God's mercy asked in prayer; Angulimala turns through his own practice, and still bears his deeds' fruit.

practice: Say out loud, quietly, the first name of one person in prison, someone you know or someone you've only read about, and then: and the people they hurt. Hold them all for a moment without deciding what anyone deserves.
If you pray, you can place them before God, as Thérèse did.

wordCard.voice: Pranzini. A condemned murderer Thérèse prayed for, who kissed the crucifix before he died.

orig.note: Greek for 'I thirst', Jesus's word from the cross in John 19:28.

carryVoice: Remember this one: my first child, because for Thérèse nobody was too far away to pray for. Until next time.
